description: From Brentwood to Mile End to Smithfield — seven weeks when ordinary people forced a king to negotiate.
content_html:
The Revolt Begins: Essex and Kent, May 1381

The immediate trigger for the Peasants’ Revolt came in late May 1381, when government tax commissioners arrived in the village of Brentwood in Essex to investigate non-payment of the Poll Tax. The villagers drove the commissioner out. News of this defiance spread rapidly. Within days, communities across Essex were in open resistance, and the rebellion in Kent was igniting in parallel. Wat Tyler emerged as the leader of the Kentish rebels, marshalling thousands into a disciplined force.

The revolt was not simply a mob. The rebels marched with organisation, targeted specific institutions (the records of serfdom, the property of corrupt officials) and articulated clear political demands. Their anger was directed not at the king himself — the fourteen-year-old Richard II was initially presented as a potential ally against bad advisers — but at the system that kept them in servitude.

Key Fact

The Peasants’ Revolt began in Brentwood, Essex in late May 1381 when tax commissioners were driven out. Within days, rebels from Essex and Kent were marching on London, led respectively by figures from each county with Wat Tyler leading the Kentish contingent.

The March on London and the Tower

By early June 1381, the rebel armies had converged on London. The city’s gates were opened by sympathisers within, and the rebels entered. They targeted properties associated with their enemies: the palace of the Savoy (belonging to John of Gaunt, the king’s uncle and the most powerful noble in England) was burned to the ground. Law courts and legal records — the documents that defined serfs’ legal obligations — were destroyed. The Tower of London was breached on 13–14 June 1381. The rebels dragged out Archbishop Sudbury — who as Lord Chancellor was associated with the hated poll taxes — and executed him on Tower Hill, along with the Lord Treasurer Robert Hales.

John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, was the most powerful noble in England and effectively one of the men guiding government during the minority of Richard II. He was widely blamed for corruption and for the direction of the failing French Wars. He also represented the most extreme end of noble privilege. Burning his palace — though the rebels reportedly forbade actual looting, turning violence towards a symbolic act of destruction rather than theft — was a powerful political statement about who the rebels held responsible for their condition.

The Meeting at Mile End, 14 June 1381

On 14 June 1381, Richard II rode out to meet the rebels at Mile End. Facing thousands of angry rebels, the fourteen-year-old king showed remarkable composure. He agreed to the rebels’ principal demands: the abolition of serfdom, a fixed low rent for land, freedom to trade, and a pardon for all the rebels. Richard even had charters drawn up on the spot granting these terms.

Many Essex rebels, satisfied that their demands had been met, began to leave London. But the revolt was not yet over. The Kentish contingent under Wat Tyler remained, with additional demands. Tyler and his followers held the city, and the key confrontation was yet to come.

Key Fact

At Mile End on 14 June 1381, Richard II promised the rebels the abolition of serfdom, the freedom to trade and a pardon for all participants. He had charters drawn up immediately — but these promises were all subsequently withdrawn after the revolt was suppressed.

Smithfield and the Death of Wat Tyler, 15 June 1381

The following day, 15 June 1381, Richard II met the Kentish rebels at Smithfield. Wat Tyler rode forward alone to present the rebels’ demands, which went beyond the concessions at Mile End: the distribution of Church wealth, the abolition of all lordship except the king’s, and equality before the law. During the tense negotiations, a confrontation broke out. Tyler was struck by the Mayor of London, William Walworth, and fatally stabbed. He died at the scene.

In the moment of confusion that followed, Richard II rode forward and addressed the rebels directly: “You shall have no captain but me.” Whether through the king’s authority, the shock of Tyler’s death, or the arrival of loyalist forces from the city, the rebel army dispersed. With Tyler dead and the leadership gone, the revolt in London collapsed.

Revolt continued in Norfolk, Suffolk, Hertfordshire and other parts of England through June 1381. Henry Despenser, Bishop of Norwich, led a military force that brutally suppressed the rebellion in East Anglia. John Ball was captured, tried and executed in July 1381. Royal commissions travelled the counties, trying and executing rebel leaders — historians estimate that several hundred people were killed in the reprisals, though precise numbers are uncertain. The charters granted at Mile End were revoked. Richard II, when pressed to honour his promises, reportedly said: “Villeins you are and villeins you shall remain.” Whether he used these exact words is disputed, but the sentiment expressed the ruling class’s determination to restore the old order.
exam_tip_html: For questions about the events of 1381, keep a clear sequence: May — revolt begins in Brentwood (Essex) and Kent; early June — rebels enter London, Savoy Palace burned, Tower breached, Archbishop Sudbury killed; 14 June — Mile End meeting, Richard II makes promises; 15 June — Smithfield, Wat Tyler killed, revolt collapses in London; July — reprisals, John Ball executed. A precise timeline shows the examiner you understand the narrative, not just isolated facts. For “explain significance” questions on the revolt’s events, always link immediate events to their longer-term consequences.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Peasants’ Revolt began in Brentwood, Essex in late May 1381 when tax commissioners were resisted; rebels from Essex and Kent converged on London, burned the Savoy Palace and breached the Tower, killing Archbishop Sudbury and the Lord Treasurer.
  • At Mile End on 14 June, Richard II promised the abolition of serfdom and a pardon for all rebels, having charters drawn up immediately; many Essex rebels left satisfied, but the Kentish force remained.
  • At Smithfield on 15 June, Wat Tyler was killed by the Mayor of London; Richard II addressed the rebels directly and the revolt collapsed; the promises made at Mile End were subsequently revoked and hundreds were executed in the reprisals.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the rebel attack on London in June 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for a simple identification, 2 for a developed feature. Example: The rebels breached the Tower of London on 13–14 June 1381 [1]; they dragged out Archbishop Sudbury (the Lord Chancellor) and Robert Hales (the Lord Treasurer) and executed them on Tower Hill [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the meeting at Mile End on 14 June 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: Richard II rode out to meet the Essex rebels and agreed to their principal demands [1]; these included the abolition of serfdom, a fixed low rent for land, freedom to trade and a general pardon, backed by written charters drawn up on the spot [1]. Feature 2: The meeting persuaded many Essex rebels to leave London, satisfied that their demands had been granted [1]; however, the Kentish rebels under Wat Tyler remained with additional demands, meaning the revolt was not yet over [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the rebels' entry into London in June 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (sympathy from Londoners who opened the gates; the king and government retreating to the Tower; the rebels' organisation and rapid march from Essex and Kent) and explains it in depth with precise factual knowledge. Secure: Identifies a cause and explains it with relevant factual support. Developing: States a cause with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the death of Wat Tyler at Smithfield on 15 June 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains a consequence in depth — the loss of the rebels' leader caused confusion; Richard II's direct address exploited the moment to disperse the crowd; the revolt in London collapsed; or the longer-term: the promises made at Mile End were all revoked, and reprisals followed across England. Secure: Explains a consequence with relevant factual support. Developing: States a consequence with limited development. Emerging: Vague point without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Richard II's role in suppressing the Peasants' Revolt.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance at the time (his personal courage at Mile End and Smithfield; his promises that dispersed the rebels; the way his authority was used by the ruling class to crush the revolt after Tyler's death) and longer-term (his subsequent revocation of all promises; the reprisals he authorised; the perception that he had both negotiated and betrayed the rebels). Precise factual knowledge throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some longer-term reference. Developing: Describes Richard's actions without clearly explaining significance. Emerging: Limited knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The death of Wat Tyler at Smithfield was the most important reason the Peasants' Revolt failed.' How far do you agree?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with precise factual knowledge. Agrees: Tyler's death removed the revolt's organising focus; the rebels were leaderless at the decisive moment; Richard II exploited the confusion immediately. Disagrees: Other factors were equally important — the ruling class had vastly greater military resources once they organised; the promises at Mile End had already split the rebel coalition by sending Essex contingents home; John Ball's subsequent capture and execution removed the revolt's ideological leadership. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Makes points for and against with evidence. Developing: Describes events without evaluating the interpretation. Emerging: Simple response; no judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Where did the Peasants' Revolt begin in late May 1381?
What happened to Wat Tyler at Smithfield on 15 June 1381?
options: He was arrested and taken to the Tower
He negotiated a peace agreement with the king
He was struck and fatally stabbed, dying at the scene
He escaped and continued leading rebels in East Anglia

knowledge_checks.q: At the _____ meeting on 14 June 1381, Richard II promised to abolish serfdom and grant a pardon to all rebels.
Archbishop _____, who was also Lord Chancellor, was seized from the Tower of London and executed by rebels on 14 June 1381.
Match each location to the key event that occurred there:
right: Where Richard II promised abolition of serfdom on 14 June 1381
Where the revolt began when tax commissioners were driven out
Where Wat Tyler was killed on 15 June 1381

flashcard_questions.q: Where and when did the Peasants' Revolt begin?
flashcard_questions.a: Brentwood, Essex, late May 1381, when tax commissioners were driven out.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the rebels do to the Savoy Palace in London?
flashcard_questions.a: They burned it to the ground — it belonged to John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster.
Archbishop of Canterbury and Lord Chancellor, executed by rebels at the Tower of London on 14 June 1381.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Richard II promise at Mile End on 14 June 1381?
flashcard_questions.a: The abolition of serfdom, freedom to trade, fixed low rents and a general pardon.

flashcard_questions.q: How old was Richard II during the Peasants' Revolt?
What happened at Smithfield on 15 June 1381?
flashcard_questions.a: Wat Tyler was killed by the Mayor of London; Richard II addressed the rebels and the revolt collapsed.

flashcard_questions.q: Who killed Wat Tyler at Smithfield?
flashcard_questions.a: William Walworth, the Mayor of London.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Richard II reportedly say when pressed to honour the Miles End promises?
flashcard_questions.a: Attributed words: 'Villeins you are and villeins you shall remain' — though the exact wording is disputed.
July 1381, after being captured following the revolt's collapse.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did many Essex rebels leave London after Mile End?
flashcard_questions.a: They believed their demands had been met and charters had been drawn up granting abolition of serfdom.

flashcard_questions.q: Who suppressed the rebellion in East Anglia after the London events?
flashcard_questions.a: Henry Despenser, Bishop of Norwich, who led a military force through the region.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to the charters granted at Mile End after the revolt was suppressed?
flashcard_questions.a: They were all revoked — Richard II withdrew every promise made to the rebels.

glossary_terms.definition: A town in Essex where the Peasants' Revolt began in late May 1381, when a tax commissioner was driven out by villagers who refused to pay the 1380 Poll Tax.
Richard II, king of England from 1377 to 1399, who met the rebels twice during the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 and made promises he subsequently broke.
The fortress in London that was attacked by the rebels on 13–14 June 1381; the Archbishop of Canterbury Simon Sudbury and others were dragged out and executed.
Archbishop of Canterbury and Lord Chancellor who was seized from the Tower of London by rebels on 14 June 1381 and executed on Tower Hill.
A field east of London where Richard II met the Essex rebels on 14 June 1381 and made promises including the abolition of serfdom, which he later withdrew.
A market area north-west of London's city walls where Richard II met Wat Tyler on 15 June 1381; the site of Tyler's killing and the decisive turning point of the revolt.

hero_image_caption: The Tower of London, breached by rebel forces during the Peasants' Revolt of June 1381.
